title: 1-Based Indexing
summary: Luau arrays start at 1, not 0. The first element is t[1], the last is t[#t], and loops run `for i = 1, #t`. Off-by-one bugs usually come from 0-based instincts.

explanation.whatItIs: Array indices count 1, 2, 3… The 'zeroth' slot doesn't participate in the array part.
explanation.whyItExists: Lua's heritage chose human counting: 'the first element' is element 1. Ecosystem consistency followed.
whenNotToUse: Writing t[0] expecting the head — that's a dictionary key, not the array
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
items = {"a", "b", "c"}
          [1]  [2]  [3]

#items = 3
items[#items] = "c"   (last)
items[0] = nil        (not part of the array!)
```
tips: Inclusive bounds everywhere: loops, sub(), random(m, n)
Negative string indices count from the end: s:sub(-1) = last char
commonMistakes: Off-by-one loops: `for i = 0, #t` overshoots with a nil at the end
Treating t[0] as special storage and confusing #t

examples.title: Bounds in practice
examples.code:
local colors = {"red", "green", "blue"}

print(colors[1])        --> red      (first)
print(colors[#colors])  --> blue     (last)

for i = 1, #colors do
    print(i, colors[i])
end

-- Cycling:
local idx = 1
local function nextColor()
    idx = idx % #colors + 1
    return colors[idx]
end
print(nextColor(), nextColor(), nextColor())   --> green blue red
